result.text: A guest enters the restaurant when feeling hungry.
He chooses a dish from the changing meal range and waits until it is his turn.
Following this he places his order with the employee.
The employee enters the order into the POS system and collects the money from the guest.
After the payment, the employee sets up a buzzer and passes it on to the guest with the following information: "When the buzzer rings, your dinner is ready".
Afterwards the employee informs the chef of the new meal order.
The chef prepares the meal and places it in the service hatch.
He then informs the employee that he has placed the finished meal in the service hatch.
As soon as the employee is aware that the meal is ready he sets off the guest's buzzer.
This is how the guest finds out that his meal is ready for collection.
He can pick up his meal and eat it.
As soon as the guest appears at the service hatch, the employee hands over his meal.
Should a guest not react to the buzzer, the employee calls for him after 5 minutes, if necessary several times in a row.

result.rule: Distinguish message tasks from message events: a task models performed work; an event models a message occurrence affecting flow.
Use bpmn:sendTask or bpmn:receiveTask when sending or waiting for a message is itself the modeled unit of work.
Use sequence flows inside one participant process and message flows between different participants. Never use sequence flow across pools.
Direct each message flow from sender to receiver. Its endpoints must belong to different pools and be valid interaction nodes.
Sequence flows may cross lanes in one process. Use message flows across participant pools, never between lanes.
Use an intermediate catch event when flow waits for a trigger and an intermediate throw event when flow emits or raises a result.

Do not model the waiting itself as a task, and do not add an event-based gateway with an additional alternative catch event unless the description names several alternative triggers.

When the description says the organization sends a request or case to an outside party and then waits for a reply from that party (such as a payment or an objection) that is received by the organization, without describing that party's own behaviour: Model the wait for the reply as an intermediate catch event in the organization's own process, placed after the request or case has been sent. Do not create a separate pool for the outside party, and do not add a message flow from the sending task to that party or from that party to the catch event.

When the description says an external party, such as a customer, performs an action (for example, providing feedback) that is optional after the case is handled, and it does not describe waiting for an incoming message, signal, time, or condition: Model that action as a task performed by that party on the optional branch, named for the action in the description's wording. Do not model it as an intermediate catch event. Reserve an intermediate catch event or event-based gateway for a wait that the description explicitly states (a message, signal, timer, or condition that must arrive before the process continues).

When The description states a step as work that a party performs, such as receiving an item or verifying a delivery, and the next described step follows it directly with no stated pause, timeout, or external occurrence being awaited.: Model that step as a task in the sequence, with the flow continuing straight to the next step. Do not replace it with an intermediate catch event. Use an intermediate catch event only where the description says the flow pauses until an external message, signal, time, or condition occurs.
